def: Aldehydes (-CHO group) and ketones (-C=O between two carbons) and carboxylic acids (-COOH group) are carbonyl compounds named using IUPAC suffixes '-al', '-one' and '-oic acid' respectively.
points: Aldehyde IUPAC name uses suffix '-al', e.g. ethanal (CH3CHO); carbon of CHO is always C1.
Ketone IUPAC name uses suffix '-one' with locant number for carbonyl position, e.g. propan-2-one (acetone).
Carboxylic acid IUPAC name uses suffix '-oic acid', e.g. ethanoic acid (CH3COOH); COOH carbon is always C1.
Aldehydes prepared by oxidation of primary alcohols (controlled, mild oxidant like PCC) or by Rosenmund reduction of acid chlorides.
Ketones prepared by oxidation of secondary alcohols, or by reaction of Grignard reagent with nitriles/acid chlorides.
Carboxylic acids prepared by oxidation of primary alcohols/aldehydes (strong oxidant like KMnO4), or by hydrolysis of nitriles/esters.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Primary alcohol"] --> B["Mild oxidation PCC"]
  B --> C["Aldehyde"]
  C --> D["Strong oxidation KMnO4"]
  D --> E["Carboxylic acid"]

example: CH3CH2OH --PCC--> CH3CHO (ethanal, mild oxidant stops at aldehyde) --KMnO4--> CH3COOH (ethanoic acid, full oxidation).
tip: Remember PCC/Rosenmund gives aldehyde (stops there), while strong oxidants like KMnO4 go all the way to acid - this control is often tested.

def: Aldehydes and ketones undergo nucleophilic addition reactions at the polar carbonyl carbon, where a nucleophile adds to carbon and a proton (or group) adds to the oxygen.
points: Carbonyl carbon is electrophilic (partial positive) due to oxygen's high electronegativity, so it attracts nucleophiles.
Addition of HCN gives cyanohydrin; addition of NaHSO3 gives bisulphite addition product.
Addition of Grignard reagent gives alcohols (primary from HCHO, secondary from other aldehydes, tertiary from ketones).
Addition of alcohols gives acetals/ketals (used to protect carbonyl group during other reactions).
Aldehydes are generally more reactive than ketones in nucleophilic addition due to less steric hindrance and less +I effect (only one alkyl group vs two).
Reactivity order: HCHO > other aldehydes > ketones, because more alkyl groups reduce electrophilicity of carbonyl carbon.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Nucleophile attacks carbonyl carbon"] --> B["Tetrahedral intermediate forms"]
  B --> C["Proton adds to oxygen"]
  C --> D["Addition product - alcohol derivative"]

example: CH3CHO + HCN -> CH3CH(OH)CN (acetaldehyde cyanohydrin), a nucleophilic addition product.
tip: State the reactivity order (HCHO > aldehydes > ketones) with the reason (steric + electronic effects) to secure full marks.

def: Aldol condensation is the reaction where two molecules of an aldehyde/ketone having alpha-hydrogen atoms combine in presence of dilute base to form a beta-hydroxy aldehyde/ketone, which can lose water to give an alpha,beta-unsaturated compound.
points: Requires at least one alpha-hydrogen atom (hydrogen on carbon next to carbonyl group) on the starting compound.
Dilute base (like NaOH) removes alpha-H to form a carbanion (enolate), which then attacks the carbonyl carbon of another molecule.
First product is an aldol (beta-hydroxy aldehyde or ketone) - hence the name aldol.
On heating/with acid, the aldol loses water (dehydration) to give an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound (condensation product).
Cross aldol condensation occurs between two different carbonyl compounds, giving a mixture of products.
This reaction is important in building longer carbon chains in organic synthesis.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Carbonyl compound with alpha-H"] --> B["Dilute base removes alpha-H"]
  B --> C["Carbanion attacks another carbonyl"]
  C --> D["Aldol - beta-hydroxy carbonyl"]
  D --> E["Heat, lose water, unsaturated carbonyl"]

example: 2 CH3CHO with dilute NaOH gives 3-hydroxybutanal (aldol), which on heating loses water to give but-2-enal (crotonaldehyde).
tip: Clearly show both steps - aldol formation AND dehydration to the unsaturated compound - partial answers lose marks.

def: Tollens' and Fehling's tests distinguish aldehydes from ketones using mild oxidation, while the iodoform test identifies compounds with a specific -CH3-CO- or -CH(OH)-CH3 group.
points: Tollens' reagent (ammoniacal AgNO3) oxidises aldehydes to carboxylic acid, forming a bright silver mirror on the test tube; ketones give no reaction.
Fehling's reagent (alkaline CuSO4 with tartrate) oxidises aldehydes, forming a brick-red precipitate of Cu2O; ketones give no reaction.
Aromatic aldehydes (like benzaldehyde) do NOT respond to Fehling's test, only aliphatic aldehydes do.
Iodoform test: compounds with CH3-CO- group (methyl ketones) or CH3-CH(OH)- group, treated with I2/NaOH, give a yellow precipitate of iodoform (CHI3).
Ethanol and acetaldehyde also give positive iodoform test since they can be oxidised to the methyl ketone type structure under the reaction conditions.
Iodoform test is used to confirm acetone, ethanol and compounds with the specific methyl carbonyl/methyl carbinol pattern.
formula: R-CHO + 2 Tollens' reagent -> R-COOH + silver mirror (Ag)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart TD
  A["Unknown carbonyl compound"] --> B["Tollens test - silver mirror if aldehyde"]
  A --> C["Fehling test - brick red precipitate if aliphatic aldehyde"]
  A --> D["Iodoform test - yellow precipitate if methyl ketone pattern"]

example: Acetone (CH3-CO-CH3) gives negative Tollens'/Fehling's test (it's a ketone) but positive iodoform test (has CH3-CO- group), forming yellow CHI3 precipitate.
tip: State clearly which test distinguishes aldehyde from ketone (Tollens'/Fehling's) and which confirms a specific structural pattern (iodoform) - don't mix their purposes.

def: Carboxylic acids are acidic because they can lose the H+ from -COOH easily, forming a carboxylate ion that is stabilised by resonance between the two oxygen atoms.
points: Carboxylic acid loses H+ to form carboxylate ion (R-COO-), which has the negative charge equally shared between both oxygen atoms by resonance.
This resonance stabilisation makes carboxylic acids much more acidic than alcohols or phenols.
Electron-withdrawing groups (like -Cl, -NO2) near the COOH group increase acidity by further stabilising the carboxylate ion.
Electron-donating groups (like -CH3) decrease acidity by destabilising the carboxylate ion.
Acidity order example: trichloroacetic acid > dichloroacetic acid > chloroacetic acid > acetic acid, due to increasing number of electron-withdrawing Cl atoms.
Carboxylic acids react with bases (NaOH, NaHCO3) to give salt and water/CO2, confirming their acidic nature; this also distinguishes them from phenols (phenols don't react with NaHCO3).
formula: R-COOH + NaHCO3 -> R-COONa + H2O + CO2 (effervescence confirms carboxylic acid)

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Carboxylic acid loses H+"] --> B["Carboxylate ion formed"]
  B --> C["Negative charge shared equally between 2 oxygens by resonance"]
  C --> D["Ion stabilised, acid is strong"]

example: Chloroacetic acid (ClCH2COOH) is more acidic than acetic acid because Cl withdraws electron density, stabilising the carboxylate ion more.
tip: Use the NaHCO3 effervescence test to distinguish carboxylic acid from phenol in your answer - a frequently asked practical distinction.

def: The Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) reaction is the alpha-halogenation of carboxylic acids using chlorine or bromine in presence of red phosphorus, replacing an alpha-hydrogen with a halogen.
points: Carboxylic acid with alpha-hydrogen reacts with X2 (Cl2 or Br2) in presence of small amount of red phosphorus.
Red phosphorus first reacts with the halogen to form phosphorus trihalide (PX3), which catalyses the reaction.
The halogen atom gets substituted specifically at the alpha-carbon (carbon next to COOH group).
Product is an alpha-halo carboxylic acid.
This reaction is useful to introduce a halogen at a specific position for further synthesis (e.g. making amino acids via substitution of the halogen).
Only acids with at least one alpha-hydrogen can undergo this reaction.

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Carboxylic acid with alpha-H"] --> B["+ X2, red phosphorus catalyst"]
  B --> C["Halogen substitutes alpha-H"]
  C --> D["Alpha-halo carboxylic acid"]

example: CH3COOH + Cl2 --(red P)--> ClCH2COOH + HCl (gives chloroacetic acid, halogen added at alpha carbon).
tip: Mention red phosphorus as the catalyst and 'alpha-carbon' specifically - naming the correct position is essential for full marks.
